findings.claim: Rule-RFC quorum=1 in single-operator mode applies equally to proposals that introduce new adopter-side bypass surfaces (new rule-config keys, new scp_bypass variants, new match-condition exclusions). A compromised or insider @jrnb2024 account can self-approve a malicious rule proposal within 48h with no second human in the loop.
findings.evidence: docs/reviews/rule-proposals/README.md §Process step 2: 'ONE approval from a SCP-CODEOWNERS member is sufficient to accept.' In single-operator mode the only CODEOWNERS member is @jrnb2024. ADOPT-001 §12.7.4 identifies .scp/rule-config.yaml as 'a bypass-surface equivalent to scp_bypass: true' and §12.7.4 Gate 2 limitation documents that verify-bypass-pairing.sh uses substring match — both show bypass surfaces already exist. RULE-TEMPLATE.md §5 explicitly solicits bypass surfaces in proposals, confirming the RFC process is the governance gate for new ones. No README.md text distinguishes proposal types by bypass-surface risk or imposes a higher window/quorum for them.
findings.impact: A rule whose match condition only fires when an opt-in flag is set (e.g., 'fires when services.yml key governance_enabled: true is present') makes absence of that flag a de-facto bypass surface. Self-approved in a MINOR release at threshold:warn, the bypass ships to all adopters before any second reviewer sees it. When the rule is later promoted to deny (a separate MAJOR proposal), the exclusion condition is established as a shipped surface that is harder to remove.
findings.mitigation: Add a paragraph to README.md §Process step 2 immediately following the quorum=1 statement: 'Exception — proposals where §5 Bypass surface is non-empty (any new .scp/rule-config.yaml key, new scp_bypass variant, or new match-condition exclusion) MUST include an explicit statement in the PR description enumerating the bypass and the operator-level control that governs it. The 48h window for such proposals is non-waivable. When a second maintainer is onboarded (D-031 escalation path, 2026-07-21), flip require_review_from_non_author: true for this proposal type.' This is documentation-enforced in single-operator mode and machine-enforced in multi-maintainer mode — symmetric with ADOPT-001 §12.7.4's two-mode breakdown.

findings.claim: RULE-TEMPLATE.md §5 'Bypass surface' solicits only three explicit surface types (new rule-config key, new scp_bypass variant, new per-finding waiver shape). It does not require enumeration of implicit bypass surfaces created by a rule's ABSENCE-OF-MATCH conditions. A proposer can truthfully answer 'None — uses existing scp_bypass three-gate + rule-config disable mechanisms' while introducing a rule that fires only under a specific affirmative condition, making the negation an unreviewed structural exclusion.
findings.evidence: RULE-TEMPLATE.md §5 text: 'Does this rule add a new bypass surface beyond the existing scp_bypass: true + three-gate model and .scp/rule-config.yaml? / New .scp/rule-config.yaml key? Name it. / New scp_bypass: <variant> flag? Name it. / New per-finding waiver shape? Name it.' The three prompts cover only mechanism-level bypass additions. None ask 'Under what inputs does this rule return allow rather than deny, and is that exclusion set intentional?' A rule like 'deny when services.yml has auth.mode: bearer_legacy AND deprecated_at is absent' is silent on services.yml files that lack auth.mode entirely — a proposer would legitimately write 'None' even though missing-auth-mode is an implicit pass.
findings.impact: Implicit bypass surfaces embedded in match conditions are harder to audit retroactively than explicit mechanism additions. Once a rule ships at threshold:warn and adopters depend on the allow-path behaviour (e.g., repos with no auth.mode field are unaffected), changing the match conditions to close the implicit exclusion is a breaking change requiring a MAJOR bump and migration guide. The RFC process is the only governance gate for catching these at design time.
findings.mitigation: Add a fourth prompt to §5 between the existing bulleted questions and the 'If the rule does NOT add...' default: '• Implicit exclusion set: under what manifest shapes does this rule return allow (pass)? Enumerate the key conditions that make a manifest exempt. If exemption = absence of a field the rule requires, state that explicitly. Reviewers should verify the exemption set is intentional and does not create an unreviewed bypass-by-omission.' The default answer remains 'None — uses existing scp_bypass three-gate + rule-config disable mechanisms' only when the rule fires on ALL manifests that reach it (i.e., the only passes are waivers and rule-config disables, not match-condition exclusions).

findings.claim: SECURITY.md is absent from the repository. The rule-regression issue template references it ('see SECURITY.md when published per WP-SCP-020 §4.1 SCP-073.sec') but SCP-073.sec is an undelivered tracked forward item. Adopters who discover a policy-bypass vulnerability have no published machine-readable disclosure channel and may default to opening a public GitHub issue, disclosing the bypass before a fix is available.
findings.evidence: .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/rule-regression.md comment block line 33: 'Security-bypass disclosures — see SECURITY.md (when published per WP-SCP-020 §4.1 SCP-073.sec) or contact @jrnb2024 privately.' ADOPT-001 §12.7.8: 'Adopters concerned about a policy-bypass disclosure should follow the SCP repo's SECURITY.md policy at https://github.com/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane (when published — WP-SCP-020 §4.1 follow-up SCP-073.sec).' docs/DECISIONS.md contains no D-NNN for SECURITY.md publication. The 020H.1 slice ships a regression-reporting surface (the issue template) that widens the window where the only disclosure guidance is an informal 'contact @jrnb2024 privately.'
findings.impact: 020H.1 ships the rule-regression issue template as a formal adopter-facing channel. That template's comment block is the first place an adopter looks for triage guidance. An adopter who finds that .scp/rule-config.yaml CODEOWNERS is absent on their repo (a known bypass surface per ADOPT-001 §11.10 MUST clause) and opens a public issue exposing it creates a public zero-day window on every other adopter who hasn't protected that path. The cross-reference to a non-existent SECURITY.md undermines the template's credibility as an authoritative disclosure guide.
findings.mitigation: Ship a SECURITY.md stub at repo root in the same release cycle as 020H.1 (or as an immediate follow-up tracked-forward item scoped within the 020H.1 sprint). Minimum content: contact address (jimbrooke@me.com or a GitHub Security Advisory email), expected initial-response SLA, statement that bypass disclosures should NOT be filed as public issues. A 10-line stub closes the gap. Update ADOPT-001 §12.7.8 and the rule-regression template comment block to drop the 'when published' qualifier. File a D-NNN in docs/DECISIONS.md recording the publication.

findings.claim: canary-replay.yml issue-body heredoc uses an unquoted EOF delimiter. REPLAY_OUTPUT undergoes bash command substitution and arithmetic expansion during body construction. Current data path does not produce injection-capable content, but this is a latent defense-in-depth gap.
findings.evidence: canary-replay.yml lines 124-163: `body="$(cat <<EOF ... ${REPLAY_OUTPUT} ... EOF)"`. The heredoc delimiter is `EOF` (unquoted), meaning any `$(...)`, backtick, or `$((...))`  within REPLAY_OUTPUT would execute during the here-document expansion. REPLAY_OUTPUT is set from `${{ steps.replay.outputs.output }}` which is the stdout of `scripts/replay-canary.sh`. That script emits tab-separated `printf` rows whose fields are `gh run list --json` values: databaseId (integer), conclusion (lowercase alphanum: success/failure/cancelled), headSha (40-char hex), createdAt (ISO 8601). None of these fields carry shell metacharacters under normal operation. The parallel `gh issue comment` step at lines 109-118 embeds REPLAY_OUTPUT in a double-quoted `--body` argument, which is safe and asymmetric with the heredoc above — a maintenance inconsistency.
findings.impact: If the replay script is extended to include gh-CLI error messages or API error bodies in REPLAY_OUTPUT (plausible for better triage), any `$(...)` in those messages executes on the runner. The blast radius is bounded by the runner's GitHub token permissions (issues: write, contents: read, actions: read) — not full repo write — but issue creation with attacker-controlled content is possible. More concretely: the asymmetry between the heredoc expansion and the safe double-quoted string in the comment step is a future-maintenance trap where a developer may assume both are equivalent.
findings.mitigation: Change the heredoc delimiter to a quoted form (`<<'ISSUE_BODY_EOF'`) and replace the `${REPLAY_OUTPUT}` interpolation with a process-substitution or temp-file approach: write REPLAY_OUTPUT to a temp file with `printf '%s\n' "${REPLAY_OUTPUT}" > "${tmpfile}"` then use `--body-file "${tmpfile}"`. This also resolves the asymmetry with the comment step. Alternatively: construct the body without a heredoc, using only safe printf format strings with `%s` placeholders and passing REPLAY_OUTPUT as a positional argument.

findings.claim: The weekly canary replay covers 'deny path' and 'waiver-suppressed deny path' but has no canary for the .scp/rule-config.yaml rule-config disable bypass path. A regression in rule-config suppress logic would go undetected by the automated cron.
findings.evidence: scripts/replay-canary.sh lines 76-79: CANARIES array contains two entries: `deliberate-violation-pre` (expected FAILURE, 1 finding, 0 waivers) and `waived-violation` (expected SUCCESS, 0 findings, 1 waiver). No entry for a fixture with `.scp/rule-config.yaml disable: true`. ADOPT-001 §12.7.4: 'Treat .scp/rule-config.yaml as a bypass-surface equivalent to scp_bypass: true.' policy-check.yml has dedicated steps for rule-config processing ('Validate rule-config against schema', 'Emit expired-rule-config one-release warning') and the Rego scp_common.rego has rule-config-aware helpers per ADOPT-001 §11.10. None of these paths are exercised by the current canary set.
findings.impact: A future refactor of scp_common.rego's rule-config helpers or of the 'Validate rule-config against schema' step could silently break disable suppression. The first detection would be an adopter filing a rule-regression issue after their CI unexpectedly starts blocking PRs whose rules they had intentionally disabled. The 4-hour rollback target in ADOPT-001 §12.7.5 assumes the regression is detected promptly; without a canary, detection latency is bounded by adopter PR volume.
findings.mitigation: Add a third canary branch: `canary/rule-config-disabled` — a branch with a deliberate SCP-R-001 violation AND a `.scp/rule-config.yaml` entry `SCP-R-001: {disable: true, justification: 'canary fixture', expires_at: 2099-12-31}`, expected outcome SUCCESS (0 effective denies, 1 disabled-rule observability record). Add the entry to CANARIES in replay-canary.sh with `expected_verdict=SUCCESS`, `expected_findings=0`, `expected_waivers=0`. Update canary-evidence.md baseline. This mirrors the two-path coverage model (deny / waived) with a third path (rule-config disabled), closing the symmetric gap.

findings.claim: The freshness-warning step reads `freshness_warning_threshold_minor` from the remote unverified main HEAD manifest rather than from the adopter's pinned manifest. The remote threshold is controlled by whoever controls main HEAD — in single-operator mode, a compromised account can set threshold=0 to spam every adopter with spurious warnings, or threshold=9999 to suppress warnings silently.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml 'Freshness warning' step: `parsed="$(printf '%s' "${main_manifest}" | python3 -c '... print(p.get("freshness_warning_threshold_minor", 2)) ...')"` then `threshold="$(printf '%s' "${parsed}" | sed -n '2p')"`. The `main_manifest` is fetched via curl from `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/main/version-manifest.json` — same as the `main_minor` version being compared. The pinned manifest at `${SCP_RUNTIME_ROOT}/version-manifest.json` is read only for `minor` (the adopter's current version), not for the threshold. version-manifest.json `_comment` field: 'The reusable workflow's freshness-warning step compares this manifest at SCP main HEAD against the manifest at the wrapper's SHA pin' — the comment implies both reads from the same document, which is what the code does, but it creates a remote-controlled threshold.
findings.impact: threshold=0 (set at main HEAD by attacker) causes every adopter to emit `SCP-FRESH-001` on every PR run regardless of their actual pin age. This is non-blocking but creates warning fatigue; adopters who add `::warning::` suppression rules in their own CI workflows to silence it also suppress legitimate future freshness alerts. threshold=9999 silently disables the warning for all adopters, removing the signal that a security-relevant release is available without adopters noticing.
findings.mitigation: Read `freshness_warning_threshold_minor` from the pinned manifest (`${SCP_RUNTIME_ROOT}/version-manifest.json`) rather than from the remote manifest. The pinned value was reviewed when the adopter last bumped their SHA — it is the adopter's intentional configuration. Use the remote manifest only for `main_minor` (which is the comparison target, not the configuration). If the pinned manifest lacks the field (pre-020H.1 pins), default to 2 (current hardcoded default). This preserves backward compat and moves the trust anchor to the verified pinned artefact.

findings.claim: canary-replay.yml gh issue create uses hardcoded `--assignee jrnb2024`. When a second maintainer onboards (D-031 escalation path, 2026-07-21 review), regression issues will continue routing to the original operator exclusively unless the workflow file is updated.
findings.evidence: canary-replay.yml line 172: `--assignee jrnb2024`. No config variable or CODEOWNERS lookup. The workflow comment block at lines 1-23 references the four-tier dispatch pattern and the triage queue but does not note the hardcoded assignee as requiring update on second-maintainer onboarding.
findings.impact: Low — this is a maintenance gap, not a security bypass. Regression issues may be missed by a second on-call maintainer if the primary operator is unavailable. Relevant to the D-031 bus-factor-1 escalation review at 2026-07-21.
findings.mitigation: Replace the hardcoded value with a config variable: add `SCP_REGRESSION_ASSIGNEE: jrnb2024` to the workflow-level env block, and reference `${SCP_REGRESSION_ASSIGNEE}` in the assignee flag. Document in the workflow comment block that this variable must be updated when a second maintainer joins. This makes the maintenance requirement explicit and searchable.

findings.claim: RULE-TEMPLATE.md §10 'Open questions' section has no guidance distinguishing bypass-relevant open questions (which should block merge) from trivially-deferrable implementation questions. A proposer can deliberately leave a bypass surface as an open question to obtain quorum approval quickly, then resolve it via amendment with less scrutiny.
findings.evidence: RULE-TEMPLATE.md §10: 'List anything the proposal leaves unresolved. Reviewers can answer these in the PR conversation; the merged proposal incorporates the resolution.' No instruction differentiates question types by bypass-surface relevance or imposes a merge-blocking condition. README.md §Process step 3 ('After merge') states the merged proposal is 'the canonical specification' — if §10 contains an unresolved bypass question, the canonical spec is ambiguous on a safety-relevant point.
findings.impact: Low independently, but compounded with SAFE-MAJ-002 (implicit bypass surfaces underspecified in §5): a proposer could deflect a reviewer's bypass concern to §10 as an open question, satisfying the 48h review window without resolving it, and then merge. The amendment PR resolving the question would have fewer eyes on it than the original proposal.
findings.mitigation: Add a note to §10: 'If any open question relates to §5 bypass surfaces or §3.1 match conditions that define an exemption set, it MUST be resolved before merge. Mark such questions with [BYPASS-RELEVANT]. If unresolved at 48h window close, the proposal auto-defers per the zero-approvals auto-defer mechanic.'

structured_review.summary: SAFETY/BYPASS lens R1 on commit 4e186e3. Three primitives reviewed: (A) rule-RFC process, (B) rollback-detection cron, (C) freshness-warning step. The freshness fetch is sound (HTTPS, Python json.load, best-effort exit-0 on all error paths, threshold public but harmless to expose). The canary-replay cron is sound for its two covered paths but has a latent heredoc injection surface and a coverage gap on the rule-config disable bypass path. The rule-RFC process exposes a structural gap: quorum=1 is acknowledged as a D-031 bus-factor-1 cost, but no higher bar exists for proposals that introduce new bypass surfaces, and RULE-TEMPLATE §5 allows a 'None' answer that can truthfully cover implicit match-condition bypasses. SECURITY.md is absent, leaving a public-issue race window for bypass-disclosure reports. Eight findings: 3 MAJ, 3 MIN, 2 nit.
structured_review.verdict_rationale: No CRIT findings. Three MAJ findings require tracked mitigations before the security posture of the three new primitives is fully sound: (1) rule-RFC quorum=1 has no heightened bar for bypass-surface-introducing proposals, (2) RULE-TEMPLATE §5 does not force enumeration of implicit match-condition-derived bypass surfaces, (3) SECURITY.md is absent while the regression template already points at it. Three MIN findings are defense-in-depth gaps (heredoc injection surface, missing rule-config canary, threshold trust chain). None of the findings require descoping. All are fixable without altering the shipped slice's observable contract.
